newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey plans central cash pool for public revenues.
newsitem.headline: Turkey plans central cash pool for public revenues.

text.p: Turkey is drawing up a central cash management system to collect public revenues under a single account in a bid to help poorer state firms finance their debts and ensure a more effective use of state funds, Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan said on Tuesday.

"All public accounts will be followed from a single centre. The aim is to eliminate the government's need to borrow," he told reporters before a meeting with senior cabinet ministers and managers of the state banks which prepared the plan.
"Under the new system, surplus money from the revenues of one government institution will be used by another which is in need of money," he said.

The plan, proposed by the Islamist Welfare Party (RP) of the two-month-old coalition government with conservatives, was hammered out by Ziraat Bank, Vakifbank, Halkbank and Emlakbank to reduce borrowing requirement of the cash-strapped treasury.
"No government institution will be allowed to invest their accounts in repo (repurchase agreement). Their money will stay in the public pool," Erbakan said.
"Therefore we will take an important step to reduce public borrowing," he said.

Analysts say profit-making state companies such as Turk Telekom, petrochemicals producer Petkim and petroleum marketer Petrol Ofisi, and almost all state banks have been investing large sums of their idle money in repo.
Repo, the trading of t-bills with maturities from overnight up to 32 days, is an attractive short-term money maker for small and large investors.
Most of the trading is made on overnight repo, which has a daily trading volume of up to 80 trillion lira.
The cash management plan aims to help overcome financial bottleneck in several public companies and institutions like social security system (SSK) and loss-making state companies.

Under the plan, a state company which needs cash will be able to draw money from the common pool instead of resorting to the treasury's borrowed funds, Erbakan said. But he did not clarify if any interest would be charged on the money drawn.
"The government's payments will be made through checques which will be cashed in this central pool," he said.
He said the system would not "disturb" budgets of the individual state companies which have "surplus" money.
The cash management would be closely monitored throughout the year to determine seasonal fluctuations in demand for the pool money, he said.

The plan is part of the government's new economic resource package, to be unveiled soon, to close big fiscal and trade deficits. The package is expected to include measures that will speed up privatisation and securitisation of state real estate.

Erbakan's first resource package, disclosed in July, included issuing foreign currency denominated bonds, sale of state property, incentives and tax excemptions for Turkish workers abroad to attract their savings into the country.
The government aims to raise $10 billion each from the two packages in the next three years.
